messages.subject: date of survey as covariate
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
I'm new to unmarked and I'm slowly formatting my data to run some
Royle (pcount) models on tiger abundance.  I had a total of 76 camera
trap locations. These were set in 4 spatially adjacent blocks, with 19
traps set for 20 days in block 1, and then those traps were taken down
and moved to the next block for 20 days, and so on.  I have input my
observations and site covariate data with no problems.  One of my
hypotheses is that detection probability varies over time due to
temperature.  Originally, I collapsed the data from 89 surveys (i.e.,
trap-nights) to 24 and included a 'block' indicator covariate to
roughly capture that temporal aspect.  It turns out that block 3 and 4
(later in the season when it is much hotter) did have a significant
negative effect on detection.  Could I 'uncollapse' the data back to
89 surveys and simply add julian date as a covariate on detection?
Although, I'm not sure how to do that since it is not a site
covariate.  I thought I could include julian date as an observation
covariate but that doesn't seem quite right.  Observation covariate
must be M x J matrix but julian date would simply be a vector with
length # of surveys.  Any help would be immensely appreciated.
Thanks.
Best,
--Neil

messages.subject: Poisson vs. negative binomial
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
I am trying to determine if I should use a Poisson or a negative
binomial model.  What indicator should I use to determine if my data
is overdispersed?  Does unmarked have a built-in method of determining
if the negative binomial is appropriate?  For instance, these are the
results from the best-fit negative binomial model I have run on my
data so far.  What exactly does the non-significant z-score tell me?
Appreciate any help.

    block4 ~ shape_am + pladj, data = tigerUMF, K = 22, mixture =
c("NB"))

(Intercept)    1.746 0.305 5.72 1.05e-08
shape_am       0.867 0.210 4.13 3.65e-05

Detection:

messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] Poisson vs. negative binomial
messages.body_plain:
hi Neil,

people would normally look at the AIC from a model that assumes a Poisson and that which assumes a NB and choose that distribution which gives clearly a lower AIC (for instance, more than 2 AIC units); see for instance our early Nmix paper in Ecol.Appl. (Kery et al. 2005). Typically, the NB turns out to be favoured by AIC. Be aware that the NB can produce very high and sometimes unrealistic abundance estimates. If that happens, I would choose the Poisson. There is a paper on those unrealistic NB abundance estimates, about 2009 or 2010 somewhere in EcolApps or perhaps ConsBiol.

Regards  --  Marc

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] offset argument and parboot
messages.body_plain:
Hi Matt,

I just double checked the code and parboot does acknowledge offsets, so I don't think there is a problem. This little simulation doesn't suggest a problem either. Are there any unusual features of the data, eg outliers?

set.seed(1032)
R <- 100
J <- 10
x1 <- rnorm(R)
x2 <- runif(R, 0.5, 1)
lam <- exp(0 + -1*x1) * x2
N <- rpois(R, lam)
table(N)
y <- matrix(NA, R, J)
for(i in 1:R) {
    y[i,] <- rbinom(J, N[i], 0.5)
}

library(unmarked)
umf <- unmarkedFramePCount(y=y, siteCovs=data.frame(x1=x1, x2=x2))
summary(umf)

(m1 <- pcount(~1 ~x1 + offset(log(x2)), umf, K=50))
pb1 <- parboot(m1, nsim=100, report=5)

> pb1

Call: parboot(object = m1, nsim = 100, report = 5)

Parametric Bootstrap Statistics:
     t0 mean(t0 - t_B) StdDev(t0 - t_B) Pr(t_B > t0)
SSE 586             48             85.8        0.257

t_B quantiles:
     0% 2.5% 25% 50% 75% 97.5% 100%
SSE 349  408 479 526 587   757  785

t0 = Original statistic compuated from data
t_B = Vector of bootstrap samples

Richard

Hi Whitney.  I think you are correct in assuming, for your categorical covariates, that noise 0, sky0, wind0, and date1 are all represented by the model's intercept.  So if you calculated estimates of pdet for sky 1, 2, and 5, they would all be relative to sky0, but not to one another.  If you wanted to change the reference level for the intercept to sky 5, for example, so you could compere the influence of sky 5 with the other levels, then you could use something like:

data=read.csv("your data",header=TRUE)
data$sky=relevel(data$sky,ref="sky5")

This is one way to generate something akin to pairwise comparisons from your model.

Richard, Andy, and Ian could diagnose your warning far more effectively than me, but I usually get that when I have missing values or not enough data to converge on an mle parameter estimate....I think. messages.body_plain:
Hi Marc,

It would be rather cruel if it was that difficult. Fortunately, you just need to create one M X T matrix and supply it as a yearlySiteCov. Continuing with the example on the help page, try this:

year <- matrix(as.character(1:5), 50, 5, byrow=TRUE)
umf <- unmarkedFramePCO(y=y, yearlySiteCovs=list(year=year), numPrimary=5)
m2 <- pcountOpen(~1, ~year, ~year, ~year, umf, K=20, control=list(trace=TRUE, REPORT=1)) # K should be higher

On a separate note, I wonder if the parameters are identifiable in this case. It shouldn't be a problem if you have "robust design" data, but I would suggest doing some simulations to check out the properties of the model when you have year-specific gamma/omega/p and no secondary samples. If you do look into this, please let us know what you find. And if you are interested in some simulation code, there are several simulation tests in a the file that comes with unmarked:  /R/library/unmarked/inst/unitTests/sim.pcountOpen.R, which is also here: https://github.com/rbchan/unmarked/blob/master/inst/unitTests/sim.pcountOpen.r .

Hope you are doing well.

Richard
